title: Case Study: Movie Booking (BookMyShow)
summary: Design a movie-ticket booking platform end to end — shows, seats, and the seat-locking mechanism that stops two users from buying the same seat.

blocks.markdown:
**Design a movie booking platform** (BookMyShow-style): browse movies by city, pick a theater and show, choose seats, and pay — with thousands of users hitting the same popular show at once.

- The functional surface looks simple; the **hard part is concurrency** — never let two users pay for the same seat on the same show.
- This builds on [concurrency-in-oo-design](concurrency-in-oo-design) and applies [lld-interview-framework](lld-interview-framework) end to end.
- The star of this case study is the **seat-locking mechanism**, not the entity list.

blocks.subTitle: Functional
blocks.markdown:
What the system must do:

- **Browse** movies by **city**, then drill into **theaters** and **shows** (a movie playing on a specific **screen** at a specific time).
- **Seat selection** — show a seat map for the chosen show with each seat's live status.
- **Booking** — reserve the selected seats and create a booking record.
- **Payment** — charge the user and confirm the booking only after payment succeeds.
- Support multiple **seat categories** (silver/gold/premium) priced differently per show.

blocks.subTitle: The core challenge
blocks.markdown:
**Non-functional requirement that shapes the whole design**: prevent **double-booking** — two users must never both end up with a confirmed ticket for the same seat on the same show.

- The danger window is between "user selects a seat" and "payment completes" — that gap can be 30 seconds or more, plenty of time for a race.
- A naive **check-then-book** (read seat status, then write) is a classic **check-then-act** race condition under concurrent requests.
- The fix isn't a bigger `if` check — it's a **temporary seat lock with expiry**, covered later in this chapter.

**Noun extraction** from the requirements:

| Noun in requirements | Becomes |
|---|---|
| city, theater, screen | `City`, `Theater`, `Screen` |
| movie, show, seat | `Movie`, `Show`, `Seat` |
| booking, payment | `Booking`, `Payment` |

Verbs matter too: "reserve for a short window" isn't a field on `Seat` — it's a behavior that becomes its own component, `SeatLockProvider`, because it needs a timer and must be checked by every concurrent request.

blocks.subTitle: City, Theater, Screen, Movie
blocks.markdown:
The browsing hierarchy — plain data holders, no business logic yet.

```text
class City:
    id: String
    name: String

class Theater:
    id: String
    name: String
    city: City
    screens: List<Screen>

class Screen:
    id: String
    theater: Theater
    seatLayout: List<Seat>       // template layout, category per seat

class Movie:
    id: String
    title: String
    durationMinutes: int
    language: String
```

blocks.subTitle: Show
blocks.markdown:
A `Show` is the actual bookable event — one movie, on one screen, at one start time. Everything a user books points back to a `Show`, not to a `Movie` or `Screen` directly.

```text
class Show:
    id: String
    movie: Movie
    screen: Screen
    startTime: DateTime
    seats: List<Seat>            // per-show copies of the screen's layout
    pricing: Map<SeatCategory, Money>

    method getSeat(seatNumber: String): Seat:
        return seats.find(s -> s.seatNumber == seatNumber)

    method availableSeats(): List<Seat>:
        return seats.filter(s -> s.status == SeatStatus.AVAILABLE)
```

blocks.subTitle: Seat & SeatStatus
blocks.markdown:
Each seat belongs to exactly one show and carries a **status** — this status field is what the whole concurrency solution revolves around.

```text
enum SeatStatus:
    AVAILABLE
    LOCKED       // temporarily held during checkout
    BOOKED       // payment confirmed

enum SeatCategory:
    SILVER
    GOLD
    PREMIUM

class Seat:
    id: String
    show: Show
    seatNumber: String
    category: SeatCategory
    status: SeatStatus = AVAILABLE
    lockedBy: String = null      // userId holding the lock, if any
    lockExpiresAt: DateTime = null
```

blocks.subTitle: Booking & Payment
blocks.markdown:
`Booking` tracks the user's intent through its lifecycle; `Payment` is a separate object so a failed charge doesn't corrupt the booking record.

```text
enum BookingStatus:
    PENDING
    CONFIRMED
    CANCELLED
    EXPIRED

class Booking:
    id: String
    user: User
    show: Show
    seats: List<Seat>
    status: BookingStatus = PENDING
    createdAt: DateTime

class Payment:
    id: String
    booking: Booking
    amount: Money
    status: PaymentStatus        // INITIATED, SUCCESS, FAILED
    method: PaymentMethod        // CARD, UPI, WALLET
```

blocks.subTitle: Why a temporary lock, not an instant book
blocks.markdown:
Booking can't be a single atomic step because **payment takes time** — the user has to enter card details or approve a UPI request, often 30–120 seconds.

- If seats stayed `AVAILABLE` during that window, another user could book the same seat and both payments could succeed — a real double-booking.
- If seats were marked `BOOKED` before payment, a user who abandons checkout would **permanently** block that seat.
- The middle ground: mark the seat `LOCKED` for a short **TTL** (time-to-live, e.g. 5 minutes). Locked seats are unavailable to others but auto-release if the user never pays.

blocks.subTitle: SeatLockProvider
blocks.markdown:
All locking logic lives in one place so no code path can bypass it — seats are never mutated directly by `Booking`.

```text
interface SeatLockProvider:
    method lockSeats(seatIds: List<String>, userId: String, ttlSeconds: int): boolean
    method releaseLock(seatIds: List<String>, userId: String)
    method confirmLock(seatIds: List<String>, userId: String)   // lock -> booked
    method isLockValid(seatId: String): boolean

class RedisSeatLockProvider implements SeatLockProvider:
    // one atomic "SET key value NX EX ttl" per seat: fails if already locked
    method lockSeats(seatIds, userId, ttlSeconds): boolean:
        acquired = []
        for seatId in seatIds:
            key = "lock:" + seatId
            if redis.setIfAbsent(key, userId, ttlSeconds):   // NX + EX, atomic
                acquired.add(seatId)
            else:
                rollback(acquired)      // release whatever we grabbed so far
                return false
        return true

    method confirmLock(seatIds, userId):
        for seatId in seatIds:
            markSeatBooked(seatId)
            redis.delete("lock:" + seatId)

    method releaseLock(seatIds, userId):
        for seatId in seatIds:
            redis.delete("lock:" + seatId)
```

blocks.subTitle: The booking flow end to end
blocks.markdown:
How `Booking`, `SeatLockProvider`, and `Payment` fit together — this is the sequence an interviewer wants you to narrate.

```text
class BookingService:
    lockProvider: SeatLockProvider
    paymentGateway: PaymentGateway

    method createBooking(user, show, seatIds): Booking:
        if not lockProvider.lockSeats(seatIds, user.id, ttlSeconds=300):
            throw SeatsUnavailableException()   // someone else holds >=1 seat

        booking = new Booking(user, show, seatIds, status=PENDING)
        save(booking)
        return booking       // client now redirects to payment

    method confirmPayment(booking: Booking, paymentResult): Booking:
        if paymentResult.isSuccess():
            lockProvider.confirmLock(booking.seatIds, booking.user.id)
            booking.status = BookingStatus.CONFIRMED
        else:
            lockProvider.releaseLock(booking.seatIds, booking.user.id)
            booking.status = BookingStatus.CANCELLED
        save(booking)
        return booking

    // background job: sweep bookings whose lock TTL passed with no payment
    method expireStaleBookings():
        for booking in findPendingOlderThan(300, "seconds"):
            lockProvider.releaseLock(booking.seatIds, booking.user.id)
            booking.status = BookingStatus.EXPIRED
            save(booking)
```

blocks.subTitle: Optimistic vs pessimistic locking
blocks.markdown:
Two ways to stop the same seat being claimed twice — both valid, different trade-offs.

| | Pessimistic locking | Optimistic locking |
|---|---|---|
| How | Lock the seat **before** letting anyone else touch it (Redis `SETNX`, DB row lock) | Let everyone read freely; write with a **version check**, reject if it changed |
| Best for | High-contention seats (front rows on a blockbuster's opening show) | Low-contention rows where collisions are rare |

Most real booking systems use **pessimistic** locking for the seat-hold step — contention is the whole point of the problem, so failing fast on a locked seat beats retrying a failed write.

blocks.subTitle: Why not just a database transaction
blocks.markdown:
**Common wrong answer**: "wrap the booking in a DB transaction and it's solved."

- A transaction protects the **write** from corruption, but it can't hold a lock across the **minutes-long gap** while a user is on a payment page — that would mean holding a DB row lock that long, which stalls every other query on that row and doesn't survive a server restart.
- The lock needs its own **expiry** independent of any single request/transaction lifecycle — that's why it lives in a separate `SeatLockProvider` (often backed by Redis with `EX`), not inside the booking transaction itself.
- The transaction still matters for the final `confirmLock` write — it's necessary, just not sufficient.

Where each pattern earns its place:

| Pattern | Where it's used |
|---|---|
| Strategy | `PricingStrategy` per seat category/show, `PaymentStrategy` per payment method |
| State | `Booking.status` transitions (PENDING → CONFIRMED / CANCELLED / EXPIRED) |
| Factory | Building the right `PaymentGateway` client for CARD / UPI / WALLET |

See [behavioral-patterns-i](behavioral-patterns-i) for Strategy and State in general form — here they replace `if/else` chains that would otherwise sit inside `BookingService`.

How the design absorbs real follow-up requirements:

- **Seat-hold countdown shown to the user** — the client just polls `lockExpiresAt` on the seats it locked; no server change needed since the TTL was already tracked.
- **Group/family booking discounts** — add a `DiscountStrategy` applied in `PricingStrategy`, no change to `SeatLockProvider` or `Booking`.
- **Trade-off**: a 5-minute lock TTL blocks a seat from everyone else even if the locking user closes the tab in 10 seconds — shorter TTLs reduce that waste but risk expiring on slow payment gateways.

blocks.subTitle: Preventing double-booking
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: How do you prevent two users from booking the same seat?**

Never let "check if free" and "mark as taken" be two separate steps — that's a check-then-act race. Make the claim atomic: an in-memory/Redis `SETNX`-style lock per seat, or a DB `UPDATE ... WHERE status = 'AVAILABLE'` and check the affected-row count. Whichever loses the race gets `false` back immediately and the client shows "seat no longer available."

blocks.subTitle: Optimistic vs pessimistic locking
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: Optimistic vs pessimistic locking — which fits seat booking?**

Pessimistic: lock the seat the moment a user selects it, so nobody else can even try. Optimistic: let both read the seat, then reject whichever write happens second via a version check. For hot shows, contention is guaranteed, so pessimistic locking (fail fast, no wasted payment attempts) beats optimistic (which would let two users both start paying, then fail one at the end).

blocks.subTitle: Why a temporary lock with expiry
blocks.markdown:
**Q: Why use a temporary lock with expiry instead of booking immediately?**

Because payment isn't instant — the user needs time to enter details or approve a UPI push. A lock with a TTL (say 5 minutes) holds the seat only long enough for that, then auto-releases if payment never completes. Without the TTL, an abandoned checkout would permanently strand a seat as unavailable.

blocks.subTitle: Modeling shows and seats
blocks.markdown:
**Q: How do you model shows and seats so pricing and status don't clash across shows?**

A `Show` is the bookable unit — one movie, one screen, one start time — and it owns its **own copy** of the seat list, not a shared reference to the screen's layout. That way seat `status` (AVAILABLE/LOCKED/BOOKED) and per-show pricing never leak between two different shows using the same physical screen.

blocks.subTitle: Where payment fits
blocks.markdown:
**Q: Where does payment fit relative to seat locking and booking?**

Payment happens strictly **after** the lock succeeds and **before** the booking is confirmed — it's the gate between `PENDING` and `CONFIRMED`. Success calls `confirmLock` (seat becomes BOOKED); failure or timeout calls `releaseLock` (seat becomes AVAILABLE again). `Payment` is its own object so a retried or failed charge never corrupts the `Booking` record directly.

blocks.subTitle: Handling an expired lock mid-payment
blocks.markdown:
**Q: What happens if the lock expires while the user is still paying?**

The background sweep (or Redis's own TTL) releases the seat back to AVAILABLE, and the booking is marked EXPIRED. If the payment gateway then reports success anyway, `confirmPayment` must re-check the lock is still held by that user before confirming — if it isn't, treat it as a failed booking and refund, rather than confirming a seat that may have been resold.

blocks.subTitle: Scaling beyond one server
blocks.markdown:
**Q: How does seat locking work once you have multiple app servers?**

An in-process lock (a language-level mutex) only protects one server's memory — useless the moment you scale horizontally. The lock must live in a **shared** store all servers can reach: Redis (`SET key val NX EX ttl`, one atomic round trip) or a database row with a `status` + `locked_until` column updated via a conditional `UPDATE`. Either way, the lock's source of truth is outside any single server's process.
